scenes.text: Visiting a lab, Neha sees a golden 'chandelier' hanging from the ceiling.
It is a dilution refrigerator; the chip at the bottom sits around 10–20 millikelvin.

steps.title: Superconducting qubits
steps.body: Circuits of aluminium/niobium with Josephson junctions behave like artificial atoms (e.g. the transmon). Controlled by microwave pulses; gates take tens of nanoseconds.

steps.title: Why so cold
steps.body: The qubit energy gap is a few GHz, tiny compared with room-temperature heat. Millikelvin temperatures keep thermal noise from flipping qubits.

steps.title: Trade-offs
steps.body:
- Fast gates, fabricated like chips
- Limited nearest-neighbour connectivity
- Coherence typically tens to hundreds of microseconds

steps.title: Not a magic box
steps.body: Most of the hardware is control electronics, wiring and cooling, not the chip.

steps.title: Trapped ions
steps.body: Charged atoms held by electromagnetic fields in vacuum; lasers or microwaves drive gates. Very high fidelities, long coherence, all-to-all connectivity in a chain, but slower gates and scaling challenges.

steps.title: Neutral atoms
steps.body: Atoms held in optical tweezers; entangled via Rydberg states. Large, reconfigurable arrays.

steps.title: Photonics
steps.body: Qubits in light; many components work at room temperature, natural for networking. Challenges: photon loss and probabilistic two-photon interactions; detectors are often cryogenic.

courses.title: Noise and quantum error correction basics
courses.summary: Where errors come from, how repetition and surface codes detect them without measuring the data, the threshold idea, and what 'logical qubit' really means.
outcomes: Learners can name bit-flip, phase-flip and readout errors
Learners can compute logical error rates for a repetition code
Learners can decode a 3-qubit syndrome

scenes.text: Ideal Bell counts are 50/50 on 00/11; hardware shows 01 and 10 too.
Noise comes from the environment, control errors and readout.

steps.title: Error types
steps.body:
- Bit flip (X error)
- Phase flip (Z error), from dephasing (T2)
- Amplitude damping (T1 decay)
- Readout error (0 read as 1)
- Leakage and crosstalk

steps.title: Mitigation vs correction
steps.body: Error **mitigation** post-processes noisy results (e.g. readout calibration, zero-noise extrapolation). Error **correction** encodes logical qubits in many physical ones and fixes errors during the computation.

steps.title: Myth
steps.body: Mitigation does not make arbitrarily long computations possible; correction is needed for that.

activity.prompt: Sort each technique

options: The measurement reports the wrong bit

scenes.text: If each bit flips with p, the code fails only if 2 or 3 flip.

steps.title: Logical error
steps.body: P_L = 3p²(1−p) + p³ = 3p² − 2p³. For p = 0.01: 0.000298, about 34× better than one bit.

steps.title: Break-even
steps.body: Encoding helps only when P_L < p, i.e. p < 0.5 for this code. Real codes have lower thresholds because gates and measurements also fail.

steps.title: Phase flips
steps.body: The bit-flip code does nothing against Z errors. Shor's 9-qubit code and the surface code handle both.

scenes.text: You can't read the data qubits: that would destroy superposition.

steps.title: Syndrome table
steps.body: (Z₀Z₁, Z₁Z₂) parity: (0,0) no error · (1,0) flip q0 · (1,1) flip q1 · (0,1) flip q2.

steps.title: Surface code
steps.body: Data and measure qubits on a 2D grid; distance-d code uses about 2d² − 1 physical qubits per logical qubit (d² data + d² − 1 measure). Below a threshold of roughly 1% physical error, increasing d suppresses logical errors exponentially.

steps.title: Milestone
steps.body: In 2024 Google reported a surface-code memory on its Willow chip whose logical error fell as code distance grew, an important below-threshold demonstration.

courses.title: Quantum cryptography: BB84 and QKD
courses.summary: How quantum key distribution uses measurement disturbance to detect eavesdroppers, with a BB84 sifting lab, the 25% error signature and the real-world limits.
outcomes: Learners can run BB84 sifting
Learners can compute the error rate an intercept-resend attacker causes
Learners can list QKD's practical limits

scenes.text: Alice sends random bits in random bases (Z: |0⟩/|1⟩, X: |+⟩/|−⟩).
Bob measures in random bases; they publicly compare bases, not bits, and keep matches.

steps.title: Protocol (Bennett & Brassard, 1984)
steps.body: 1. Alice picks random bits and bases. 2. Bob picks random bases. 3. Compare bases over an authenticated public channel. 4. Keep bits where bases match (~50%). 5. Sacrifice some to estimate errors. 6. Error correction and privacy amplification.

steps.title: Sifting
steps.body: Bits 1 0 1 1, Alice Z X X Z, Bob Z Z X X → keep positions 1 and 3 → key '11'.

steps.title: Authentication
steps.body: The classical channel must be authenticated, or a man-in-the-middle wins.

scenes.text: Eve measures each photon in a random basis and resends it.

steps.title: Why 25%
steps.body: Eve picks the wrong basis half the time; then Bob gets a random result, wrong half the time: ½ × ½ = ¼.

steps.title: Detect
steps.body: If Alice and Bob compare 200 sifted bits and see ~50 errors, abort. Typical honest QBER on real links is a few percent.

steps.title: Privacy amplification
steps.body: Below a security threshold (around 11% for BB84 in standard proofs), they can still distil a shorter secret key.

scenes.text: Satellite experiments (e.g. China's Micius, launched 2016) distributed entangled photons over 1,000+ km.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body:
- Photon loss limits fibre distance to roughly hundreds of km without trusted nodes
- Needs dedicated hardware and an authenticated channel
- Implementation attacks on detectors have been demonstrated
- Gives key exchange only, not signatures

steps.title: QKD vs PQC
steps.body: QKD uses physics and special hardware. Post-quantum cryptography is new maths running on ordinary computers. Several national security agencies currently prefer PQC for most uses.

steps.title: Not unbreakable in practice
steps.body: 'Provably secure' applies to the ideal protocol; real devices have side channels.

scenes.text: NIST published FIPS 203, 204 and 205 in August 2024.
They replace public-key schemes that Shor would break.

steps.title: The three standards
steps.body:
- **FIPS 203 ML-KEM** (from CRYSTALS-Kyber): key encapsulation, lattice-based (Module-LWE)
- **FIPS 204 ML-DSA** (from CRYSTALS-Dilithium): digital signatures, lattice-based
- **FIPS 205 SLH-DSA** (from SPHINCS+): stateless hash-based signatures, conservative backup

steps.title: What stays
steps.body: Symmetric crypto (AES) and hashes (SHA-2/SHA-3) stay; use larger parameters (AES-256) for long-term security against Grover.

steps.title: Not quantum
steps.body: PQC algorithms run on classical computers; no quantum hardware is needed.

scenes.text: X25519 public key: 32 bytes. ML-KEM-768 public key: 1,184 bytes; ciphertext 1,088 bytes.
Browsers already deploy hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM key exchange.

steps.title: Hybrid
steps.body: Combine a classical and a post-quantum KEM so the session stays secure if either holds. Common today in TLS 1.3 as X25519MLKEM768.

steps.title: Size ratio
steps.body: 1,184 ÷ 32 = 37: the PQ public key is 37× larger, but still small enough for a TLS handshake.

steps.title: Gotchas
steps.body: Larger ClientHello messages have broken some old middleboxes; test your network path.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview · Quantum software engineer (fresher)

scenes.text: A startup interviews Ravi for a junior quantum software role.
Five rounds: concepts, simulator design, Grover, Shor/PQC and a behavioural question.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Define → explain → example → limits. Draw a circuit if you can.

steps.title: What they assess
steps.body: Correct fundamentals, clear communication, testing habits and honesty about hype.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: Saying 'a qubit is 0 and 1 at the same time' with no maths behind it.

rounds.q: Explain what a qubit is to a software engineer who knows only classical bits.
rounds.model: A qubit is a two-level quantum system described by a unit vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with complex amplitudes. Measuring it gives 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with |β|², and afterwards the state is the observed basis state. Gates are unitary matrices that rotate the state, which I picture on the Bloch sphere. The power comes from interference between amplitudes, not from storing many answers at once.
followups: What is the difference between global and relative phase?

rounds.q: Write out how you would implement a single-qubit gate on qubit t in an n-qubit state-vector simulator.
rounds.model: I store 2ⁿ complex amplitudes. For every index i whose bit t is 0, I pair it with j = i | (1 << t), read both old amplitudes, and write U applied to that pair back. That is O(2ⁿ) per gate. I test it with known circuits like H·H = I and the Bell state.
followups: How does memory scale at 30 qubits?

rounds.q: How does Grover's algorithm work and how many iterations would you use for N = 1,024 and one solution?
rounds.model: Start in a uniform superposition. The oracle flips the sign of the marked state and the diffusion operator reflects all amplitudes about their mean; together they rotate the state by 2θ toward the solution, where sin θ = 1/√N. The optimal count is about (π/4)√N, so for N = 1,024 about 25 iterations. More than that overshoots and the success probability falls.

rounds.q: What does Shor's algorithm threaten, and how would you advise a company today?
rounds.model: Shor's algorithm factors and computes discrete logarithms efficiently, which breaks RSA, Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography, but only on large fault-tolerant machines that don't exist yet. Because recorded traffic can be decrypted later, I'd advise a cryptographic inventory, prioritising long-lived data, piloting hybrid key exchange with ML-KEM and planning signature migration to ML-DSA, with crypto-agility throughout.

rounds.q: Tell me about a time you found a bug in your own analysis. How did you catch it?
rounds.model: In my simulator project, my Bell circuit gave the right probabilities but my QFT output had wrong phases. I wrote a test comparing against a direct DFT formula and found I had the qubit ordering reversed. I fixed it, documented the convention, and added the test to CI so it couldn't regress.

tips: Be honest about hype and limits

quiz.q: Best structure for a technical answer:
When unsure in an interview you should…
options: Say what you know and how you'd find out

rounds.q: A Bell-state experiment on hardware shows 8% of counts in 01 and 10. Walk me through your diagnosis.
rounds.model: First I'd separate readout from gate errors by running calibration circuits for |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩ and building a readout matrix. Then I'd check the transpiled circuit for extra SWAPs and the device's current CNOT error on those qubits. Running a noisy simulation with the backend's noise model tells me whether 8% is expected. If not, I'd move to better qubits or report a calibration issue.
followups: How would you verify entanglement, not just correlation?

rounds.q: Explain the surface code's threshold and why logical qubits need so many physical qubits.
rounds.model: The surface code places data and measure qubits on a grid and repeatedly measures parity checks; the syndromes reveal errors without measuring the logical information. A distance-d patch uses about 2d² − 1 physical qubits and corrects up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors. If physical error rates are below a threshold of roughly 1%, increasing d suppresses the logical error rate exponentially, so we trade many physical qubits for one reliable logical qubit.

rounds.q: Our TLS handshakes fail for some branch offices after enabling hybrid ML-KEM. What do you do?
rounds.model: Hybrid ML-KEM makes the ClientHello larger, and some older middleboxes mishandle it. I'd capture traffic at an affected branch, confirm where the handshake breaks, and identify the device. Short term, allow a controlled fallback for that path; long term, update or replace the device with the vendor. I'd continue a staged rollout with monitoring.
followups: How do you avoid weakening security with fallback?

rounds.q: Why are you interested in quantum technology, and how do you keep up with it honestly?
rounds.model: I'm drawn to quantum because it combines linear algebra, physics and engineering, and the security side has real urgency today. I follow peer-reviewed papers and preprints, official standards like NIST's, and I try to reproduce results in simulation. I'm sceptical of press releases and always ask what the classical baseline is.

rounds.q: Design a 2-week benchmark comparing QAOA with classical MaxCut heuristics.
rounds.model: I'd generate graph families of increasing size, compute exact optima for small ones by brute force, and run strong classical heuristics like simulated annealing or Goemans–Williamson. Then QAOA at p = 1–3 in simulation and on hardware, measuring approximation ratio, wall-clock time and total shots. I'd report all results including where QAOA loses.
followups: How do you pick γ and β?

lessons.title: The CIA triad: what security protects

scenes.text: At a school in Ranchi, a spreadsheet of Class 10 pre-board marks was accidentally shared to a public link. Parents saw other children's marks.
Days later, someone with the link quietly changed a few marks. Then the school's website went down on results day under heavy traffic.
The computer teacher, Mr. Minz, used it to teach his class: 'Three different failures. Confidentiality broken by the leak, integrity broken by the edits, availability broken by the outage.'

steps.title: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
steps.body:
- **Confidentiality:** only the right people can see information. Tools: access control, encryption, classification ('internal', 'confidential').
- **Integrity:** information is accurate and not changed without authorisation. Tools: permissions, hashing, digital signatures, version history, audit logs.
- **Availability:** systems and data are there when needed. Tools: backups, redundancy, capacity planning, DDoS protection, patching.
Most security decisions balance these three. Locking a file so tightly that doctors cannot open it in an emergency protects confidentiality but harms availability.

steps.title: AAA and non-repudiation
steps.body:
- **Authentication:** proving who you are (password, OTP, fingerprint).
- **Authorisation:** what you are allowed to do once identified (read marks vs edit marks).
- **Accounting (auditing):** recording who did what and when (logs).
- **Non-repudiation:** someone cannot credibly deny an action they took — e.g. a digitally signed document.

steps.title: Risk in one line
steps.body:
**Risk ≈ likelihood × impact.** A threat (someone or something that could cause harm) exploits a vulnerability (a weakness) to damage an asset (something of value).
Responses to a risk: **mitigate** (add controls), **transfer** (insurance, outsourcing), **avoid** (stop the risky activity), **accept** (consciously live with it).

steps.title: Worked example: fixing the school's problems
steps.body:
- Confidentiality: share marks only with named staff accounts, never 'anyone with the link'; parents see only their own child's marks through a login.
- Integrity: only the exam cell can edit; keep version history; log every change.
- Availability: host results on a service that can scale; publish a backup PDF link; test with expected traffic beforehand.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of your phone. Write one threat to each of its confidentiality, integrity and availability, and one control you already use (or should) for each.

activity.prompt: Which part of the CIA triad was mainly harmed?

items.text: A hacker reads customers' Aadhaar-linked records
Someone edits bank account numbers in invoices
An email with salary data goes to the wrong person
A website crashes during a flash sale
Exam marks are changed without permission

quiz.why: Encryption protects confidentiality: only someone with the key can read the data.
Backups mainly protect availability, because you can restore data after loss. They also help recover integrity after damage.

quiz.q: Checking what a logged-in user may do is…
quiz.why: Checking what a logged-in user is allowed to do is authorisation. Authentication is proving who they are.

quiz.q: Buying cyber insurance is an example of risk…
quiz.why: Buying cyber insurance shifts the financial impact to the insurer, which is risk transfer.

quiz.q: Logs that record who changed a mark support…
quiz.why: Logs that record who changed a mark support accounting (auditing), because actions can be traced to a person.

scenes.text: Accountant Manoj in a Kanpur textile firm received a WhatsApp message: 'Your courier is on hold. Download the delivery form.' The file was named Delivery_Form.apk.
He installed it. The app asked for SMS permission. Within hours, OTPs were being read and small amounts drained from linked wallets.
The firm's IT person, Fatima, wiped the phone, reset passwords and helped him report it. Then she trained the whole office: unexpected files, urgency and requests for permissions are red flags.

steps.title: Malware types
steps.body:
- **Virus:** attaches to files/programs and spreads when they run.
- **Worm:** spreads by itself across networks, without user action.
- **Trojan:** looks legitimate (a 'delivery form' app) but hides malicious functions.
- **Ransomware:** encrypts or steals data and demands payment.
- **Spyware / keylogger:** secretly collects information or keystrokes.
- **Rootkit:** hides deep in the system to keep privileged access.
- **Botnet:** many infected devices controlled remotely, e.g. for DDoS attacks or spam.
- **Fileless malware:** runs in memory or abuses legitimate tools, leaving fewer traces.

steps.title: Social engineering
steps.body:
Attackers manipulate people rather than machines, using **urgency, fear, authority, curiosity or greed**.
- **Phishing** (email), **smishing** (SMS), **vishing** (voice calls), plus messaging apps.
- **Spear phishing:** targeted at a specific person using personal details; **whaling:** targets senior executives.
- **Pretexting:** an invented story ('I'm from your bank's KYC team').
- **Baiting:** a free USB drive or a 'free movie' download.
- **Tailgating/piggybacking:** following someone through a secure door.
- **Business email compromise:** fake or hijacked email from a 'vendor' changing bank details.

steps.title: Other common attacks
steps.body:
- **Denial of service (DoS/DDoS):** overwhelm a service so real users can't reach it.
- **Man-in-the-middle / on-path:** intercepting traffic, e.g. on fake Wi-Fi.
- **Credential stuffing:** using leaked passwords from one site on others.
- **Brute force / password spraying:** guessing many passwords, or one common password across many accounts.
- **Supply-chain attacks:** compromising software or vendors that many organisations trust.
- **Zero-day:** exploiting a vulnerability before a fix exists.

steps.title: Everyday defences
steps.body:
- Install apps only from official stores; be wary of APK files sent in chats.
- Keep OS and apps updated; enable automatic updates.
- Use a password manager and **unique** passwords; turn on MFA.
- Back up important data (with one copy offline) — the best answer to ransomware.
- Pause before acting on urgent messages; verify through an official number or app.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check which apps on your phone have SMS, accessibility or 'display over other apps' permissions. Remove any you don't trust — these permissions are commonly abused by banking trojans.

quiz.q: Malware that spreads without any user action is a…
quiz.why: A worm spreads on its own across networks, without needing any user action. A virus usually needs a user to run something.

quiz.q: A targeted email to the CFO using details from LinkedIn is…
quiz.why: A targeted email to a senior executive such as the CFO, using personal details, is whaling or spear phishing.

quiz.q: Best defence against ransomware destroying your data?
options: Tested backups including an offline copy
quiz.why: The best defence against ransomware is tested backups, including an offline copy, so you can restore without paying.

quiz.q: Attackers try 'Password@123' on thousands of accounts. This is…
quiz.why: Password spraying tries one common password on many accounts. It avoids lockouts that trying many passwords on one account would cause.

quiz.q: Which emotion do social engineers most often exploit?
quiz.why: Social engineers use urgency and fear, because pressure short-circuits careful thinking.

lessons.title: Phishing, scams and what to do if it happens

scenes.text: Retired teacher Mrs. Shanta in Mysuru got a call: 'Your bank KYC expires today. Your account will be blocked. Tell me the OTP we just sent to verify.'
She remembered her granddaughter Riya's rule: 'No genuine bank asks for your OTP, PIN or password. Ever.' She hung up.
She called the number printed on her debit card. The bank confirmed it was a scam. Riya helped her report the caller's number on the national cybercrime portal.

steps.title: How to spot phishing
steps.body:
Red flags:
- **Urgency or threats:** 'account blocked in 2 hours', 'police case filed'.
- **Requests for secrets:** OTP, UPI PIN, passwords, CVV, screen-sharing or remote-access apps.
- **Look-alike senders and links:** amaz0n-offers.co, sbi-kyc-update.in; shortened links hiding the destination.
- **Too good to be true:** lottery wins, huge discounts, work-from-home 'tasks' that pay at first, then ask for 'deposits'.
- **Unexpected attachments** or QR codes.
Hover over (or long-press) links to see the real address; when in doubt, open the official app or type the website yourself.

steps.title: UPI and payment scams in India
steps.body:
- You **never** need to enter your UPI PIN to **receive** money. A 'collect request' asking for your PIN is a payment *from* you.
- Never share OTPs or install screen-sharing apps at a stranger's request.
- Scanning a QR code is for paying, not receiving.
- 'Digital arrest' calls — fake police or officials on video calls demanding money — are a scam; genuine agencies don't arrest people over video calls or demand transfers.
- Fake customer-care numbers appear in search results and social media; get numbers only from official apps, websites or your card.

steps.title: If you've been scammed — act fast
steps.body:
- **Call 1930** (national cybercrime helpline) and report at **cybercrime.gov.in** as soon as possible — quick reporting improves the chance of freezing money in transit.
- Inform your bank through its official number; block cards/UPI if needed.
- Change passwords (starting with email), turn on MFA, log out other sessions.
- Keep evidence: screenshots, transaction IDs, numbers, links.
- For immediate danger, call **112**.
Outside India, contact your bank and your country's official cybercrime reporting channel.

steps.title: At work: business email compromise
steps.body:
A 'vendor' emails: 'Our bank details have changed, please pay the new account.' Rules that stop most losses:
- Verify any change of bank details by calling a **known** number (not one in the email).
- Two-person approval for new payees and large payments.
- Report suspicious emails with the 'report phishing' button so the security team can block them for everyone.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Teach one family member the three golden rules today: never share OTP/PIN, verify via official numbers, and report on 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in.

a.text: You receive an SMS: 'Your electricity will be disconnected tonight. Call 98xxxxxx12 immediately.' What do you do?

choices.label: Call the number in the SMS
choices.feedback: Scammers use urgent bill-disconnection messages to get you on the phone.

choices.label: Check the bill in the official app/website or call the official number on your bill
choices.feedback: Correct — verify through a channel you trust.

b.text: The 'officer' asks you to install a remote-support app to 'update your meter'. What now?

choices.label: Hang up — remote-access apps give full control of your phone
Install it to avoid disconnection
choices.feedback: This lets the scammer see your screen and OTPs.

c.text: Your bill is fully paid; the SMS was fake. You report the number on cybercrime.gov.in and warn your family group.

choices.label: Finish

d.text: Money leaves your account. What first?

choices.label: Call 1930 immediately, inform the bank, uninstall the app, change passwords
choices.feedback: Fast reporting improves the chance of recovery.

e.text: Rule learned: urgency + unknown number + requests for apps, OTPs or PINs = scam. Verify through official channels and report quickly.

quiz.q: Do you need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money?
quiz.why: You never need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money. The PIN is needed only to pay, so a request asking for it is a scam.

quiz.q: India's national cybercrime helpline number is…
quiz.why: India's national cybercrime helpline is 1930. You can also report at cybercrime.gov.in.

quiz.q: A 'vendor' emails new bank details. Best action?
options: Reply to the email asking if it's real
Verify by calling a known number before changing anything
quiz.why: If a vendor emails new bank details, verify by calling a known number before changing anything. Replying to the same email may reach the scammer.

quiz.q: Which link is most suspicious for a bank?
options: The URL typed from your passbook
quiz.why: 'sbi-kyc-update-now.in' is a look-alike domain that uses urgency. The bank's real address is the one from your passbook, card or official app.

quiz.q: A stranger asks you to install a screen-sharing app. Risk?
options: They can see OTPs and control your phone
quiz.why: A screen-sharing app lets a stranger see your screen, including OTPs, and control your phone. Remote access is a top scam tool.

lessons.title: Passwords, MFA and the cryptography behind the padlock

scenes.text: College student Rohit used the same password for email, a gaming site and his food app. The gaming site was breached; his password was published online.
Attackers tried it everywhere — credential stuffing. They got into his email and reset his other passwords.
His friend Ayesha helped him recover: a password manager with unique passwords, MFA with an authenticator app, and an explanation of how websites should store passwords (hashed, never in plain text).

steps.title: Strong authentication
steps.body:
- **Length beats complexity:** a passphrase like 'mango-kite-river-42-chalk' is strong and memorable.
- **Unique password per site** — use a password manager.
- **MFA (multi-factor):** combine factors — something you know (password), have (phone, security key), are (fingerprint). Authenticator apps and hardware security keys (FIDO2/passkeys) resist phishing better than SMS codes, but any MFA is far better than none.
- **Passkeys:** passwordless sign-in using cryptographic keys stored on your device; resistant to phishing.

steps.title: Hashing
steps.body:
A **hash function** turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint (e.g. SHA-256 gives 256 bits). Same input → same hash; a tiny change → a completely different hash; you can't reverse it to get the input.
Uses: checking file integrity (compare the published hash of a download), digital signatures, and **storing passwords**.
Passwords must be stored with slow, **salted** password-hashing algorithms (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2). A **salt** is a random value per user so identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables don't work.

steps.title: Encryption: symmetric and asymmetric
steps.body:
- **Symmetric encryption** (e.g. AES): the same secret key encrypts and decrypts. Fast; used for bulk data. Problem: sharing the key safely.
- **Asymmetric encryption** (e.g. RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography): a **public key** (share with anyone) and a **private key** (keep secret). Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key.
- **Digital signature:** sign with your *private* key; anyone verifies with your *public* key — proves authenticity and integrity (supports non-repudiation).
- **Certificates** bind a public key to an identity (a website's domain), issued by a trusted certificate authority.

steps.title: Worked example: what happens behind the padlock (TLS)
steps.body:
When you open https://yourbank.example:
- Your browser and the server agree on TLS settings.
- The server sends its **certificate**; your browser checks it's valid for that domain and signed by a trusted authority.
- They use asymmetric cryptography (key exchange) to agree on fresh **symmetric session keys**.
- All page data is then encrypted with fast symmetric encryption and integrity-checked.
The padlock means the connection is encrypted to that domain — **not** that the site is honest. Phishing sites can have padlocks too.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing hashing (one-way) with encryption (reversible with a key).
- Storing passwords with fast hashes like plain MD5/SHA-1 or without salt.
- Thinking 'https' means 'safe site'.
- Writing your own cryptography — use well-tested libraries and standard protocols.
- Approving MFA prompts you didn't start ('MFA fatigue' attacks) — deny and change your password.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Turn on MFA for your main email account today and save the backup codes somewhere safe offline. Then check a breach-notification service your browser or password manager offers to see if your email appears in known breaches.

statements.s: Hashing is reversible if you know the key.
statements.why: Hashes are one-way; encryption uses keys.

statements.s: A salt makes identical passwords produce different stored hashes.
statements.why: Each user gets a random salt.

statements.s: A digital signature is created with the signer's private key.
The padlock icon proves a website is trustworthy.
statements.why: It proves an encrypted connection to that domain only.

statements.s: TLS uses symmetric encryption for the bulk of the data.
statements.why: Asymmetric is used to set up keys and authenticate.

statements.s: SMS OTP is the most phishing-resistant MFA method.

options: A unique long passphrase stored in a password manager, with MFA
quiz.why: The strongest choice is a unique, long passphrase stored in a password manager, with MFA. Names, birth years and phone numbers are easy to guess.

options: Salted, slow password hashing such as bcrypt or Argon2
quiz.why: Websites should store passwords with salted, slow password hashing such as bcrypt or Argon2. Plain text, Base64 or reversible encryption can be undone.
AES is symmetric encryption: the same key is used to encrypt and decrypt.

quiz.q: To verify a signed document you use the signer's…
quiz.why: A signature is made with the signer's private key and verified with the signer's public key.

quiz.q: You get an MFA prompt you didn't initiate. Do what?
options: Deny it and change your password
quiz.why: An MFA prompt you didn't start means someone may have your password. Deny it and change your password.

questions.q: The 'C' in the CIA triad stands for…
questions.why: In the CIA triad, C stands for Confidentiality: only authorised people can see the data.

questions.q: Which is an example of MFA?
questions.why: MFA uses different types of factors, such as something you know (password) and something you have (authenticator code). Two passwords are the same type.

questions.q: A fake 'bank' SMS with a link is…
questions.why: A fake bank SMS with a link is smishing (SMS phishing). Vishing is by voice call.

questions.q: What should you never share with anyone, including 'bank staff'?
questions.why: Never share your OTP or UPI PIN with anyone, including people who claim to be bank staff. No genuine bank asks for them.
A DDoS attack overwhelms a service with traffic, so it mainly targets availability.

questions.q: A program disguised as a game that steals data is a…
questions.why: A program disguised as something useful, like a game, that steals data is a Trojan.

questions.q: Why are salts used in password storage?
options: So identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed attacks fail
questions.why: A salt is random data added to each password before hashing. Identical passwords then get different hashes, and precomputed attacks fail.

questions.q: In TLS, the server's certificate mainly proves…
options: The public key belongs to that domain
questions.why: A TLS certificate proves that the public key belongs to that domain. It doesn't mean the site is honest or bug-free.
Risk is commonly estimated as likelihood × impact.

questions.q: A user's password leaked from one site is used to log in to another. This is…
questions.why: Using a password leaked from one site to log in to another is credential stuffing. It works because people reuse passwords.

questions.q: Which MFA method is most resistant to phishing?
questions.why: A FIDO2 security key or passkey is bound to the real site's origin, so it won't work on a fake site. SMS and email codes can be phished.

questions.q: Signing a contract digitally with your private key provides…
options: Integrity, authenticity and support for non-repudiation
questions.why: A digital signature made with your private key shows integrity (not changed), authenticity (from you) and supports non-repudiation. Anyone with your public key can verify it.

questions.q: Victim of an online payment fraud in India — the best immediate step?
options: Call 1930 / report on cybercrime.gov.in and inform the bank quickly
Pay the scammer again to get money back
questions.why: Speed helps freezing the funds. Call 1930 or report on cybercrime.gov.in, and inform the bank quickly. Never pay the scammer again.

scenes.text: A student researcher, Tanya, emailed an ed-tech company in Bengaluru: 'By changing the number in /api/reports/1042 to 1043, I can see another student's report card.'
Lead developer Arjun checked: true. The API checked that users were logged in, but not *whose* report they were requesting.

Fixing it took an hour. Arjun then used the OWASP Top 10 as a checklist to review the whole app — and found three more issues before attackers did. They thanked and rewarded Tanya through their disclosure programme.

steps.title: What OWASP is
steps.body: **OWASP** (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is a non-profit community producing free security guidance. The **OWASP Top 10** is an awareness list of the most critical web application security risk categories, updated every few years (the 2021 edition is used here — check for newer editions). It's a starting point, not a complete standard; for detailed requirements see the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS).

steps.title: OWASP Top 10 (2021)
steps.body:
- **A01 Broken Access Control:** users act outside their permissions (Tanya's report card = an IDOR, insecure direct object reference).
- **A02 Cryptographic Failures:** sensitive data exposed due to weak or missing encryption.
- **A03 Injection:** untrusted input interpreted as code — SQL, OS command, LDAP injection; XSS is included here.
- **A04 Insecure Design:** flaws in the design itself (no rate limit on OTP attempts).
- **A05 Security Misconfiguration:** default passwords, verbose errors, open cloud storage.
- **A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components:** old libraries with known vulnerabilities.
- **A07 Identification and Authentication Failures:** weak login, session handling, credential stuffing.
- **A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures:** untrusted updates, insecure deserialisation, compromised CI/CD.
- **A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures:** attacks go unnoticed.
- **A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF):** the server is tricked into fetching attacker-chosen URLs (e.g. internal cloud metadata).

steps.title: Worked example: fixing the IDOR
steps.body:
Vulnerable (pseudo-code):
GET /api/reports/:id → return db.reports.find(id)

Fixed:
GET /api/reports/:id →
  report = db.reports.find(id)
  if report.student_id != currentUser.id and not currentUser.isTeacherOf(report.student_id): return 403
  return report

Rule: **check authorisation on the server for every object, every request** — hiding buttons in the UI is not access control.

steps.title: Ethics and law
steps.body: Only test systems you own or have **written permission** to test (a bug bounty or a lab). Unauthorised access to computer systems is a crime in India (under the Information Technology Act, 2000) and in most countries. Practise on deliberately vulnerable training apps such as OWASP Juice Shop in your own environment. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick any web app you've built (or a tutorial app). For each OWASP category, write one question you'd ask about it, e.g. A01: 'Can user A access user B's data by changing an ID?'

activity.prompt: Match the incident to its OWASP Top 10 (2021) category.
pairs: Changing an ID in the URL shows another user's order
Admin console reachable with default password admin/admin
App uses a library version with a published critical CVE
Server fetches a user-supplied URL and reveals internal cloud metadata
Attack ran for months with no alerts or logs
A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

quiz.q: Which category ranked #1 in the OWASP Top 10 (2021)?
quiz.why: In the OWASP Top 10 (2021), Broken Access Control is ranked #1 (A01), the most common serious web risk.

quiz.q: Hiding the 'Delete' button from non-admins is enough access control. True?
quiz.why: This is false. Hiding a button doesn't stop someone sending the request directly. The server must enforce permissions.

quiz.q: No limit on OTP attempts, allowing guessing, is best described as…
quiz.why: No limit on OTP attempts is a missing control in the design, which allows guessing. It's an insecure design or authentication failure.

quiz.q: Before security-testing a website, you need…
options: Written permission from the owner (or an authorised bug bounty scope)
quiz.why: Before security-testing a site you need written permission from the owner, or an authorised bug-bounty scope. Unauthorised testing is illegal.
IDOR stands for Insecure Direct Object Reference: objects are reached by guessable references, like IDs, without access checks.

story.title: The search box that dumped a database

scenes.text: A small travel portal built its search like this: "SELECT * FROM hotels WHERE city = '" + city + "'".
An attacker typed: x' UNION SELECT email, password_hash FROM users -- and the results page showed user emails and password hashes.
Developer Leela rewrote every query with parameters, added output encoding and a Content Security Policy. A later penetration test found nothing in those areas.

steps.title: SQL injection and the fix
steps.body:
Injection happens when **data is mixed into code**. In the story, the attacker's quote character ended the string and added their own SQL.
**Fix: parameterised queries (prepared statements)** — the query structure is fixed, and input is sent separately as data:
- Python: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM hotels WHERE city = %s', (city,))
- Node (pg): client.query('SELECT * FROM hotels WHERE city = $1', [city])
Also: least-privilege database accounts, input validation (allow-lists for things like sort columns), and ORM safe APIs. Escaping by hand is error-prone; parameters are the primary defence.

steps.title: Command injection
steps.body: Never build shell commands from user input: os.system('ping ' + host) lets someone enter '8.8.8.8; rm -rf /'. Use library functions or pass arguments as a list without a shell (subprocess.run(['ping', '-c', '1', host])) and validate input against strict patterns.

steps.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
steps.body:
XSS = attacker-controlled script runs in *other users'* browsers on your site, letting it steal session data or act as the user.
- **Stored XSS:** malicious input is saved (a review, a comment) and shown to others.
- **Reflected XSS:** input in a URL is echoed back in the page.
- **DOM-based XSS:** client-side JavaScript writes untrusted data into the page unsafely (e.g. innerHTML).
Defences:
- **Context-aware output encoding** (templating engines that auto-escape; textContent instead of innerHTML).
- Sanitise rich HTML with a vetted library if you must allow formatting.
- **Content Security Policy (CSP)** header to restrict where scripts can come from.
- **HttpOnly** cookies so scripts can't read session cookies.

steps.title: Worked example: encoding in action
steps.body: A user's review contains a script tag. With auto-escaping, the page receives the text with < and > converted to < and > — the browser *displays* the characters instead of running them. With innerHTML or an unescaped template, the browser would execute it. Same data, opposite outcomes: the difference is how you output it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'We validate on the frontend' — attackers call your API directly.
- Blacklisting words like 'script' — attackers have many other payloads.
- Using string concatenation for 'just this one quick query'.
- Disabling auto-escaping in templates to 'fix formatting'.
- Building dynamic table/column names from input without an allow-list (parameters can't bind identifiers).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In a local practice app (never on a real site), find every place where SQL is built with + or f-strings and rewrite it with parameters. Then search the frontend for innerHTML and replace with textContent where possible.

activity.prompt: Complete the safe, parameterised query (Python DB-API style).
activity.text:
cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ___', (email,))
# and in the browser, show user text with element.___ = comment

quiz.why: Parameterised queries keep SQL code separate from user data, so input can't change the query. This is the primary defence against SQL injection.

quiz.q: A malicious comment saved in the database runs in every visitor's browser. This is…
quiz.why: A malicious comment saved in the database that runs in every visitor's browser is stored XSS, because the payload persists.

quiz.q: Which cookie flag stops JavaScript from reading the session cookie?
quiz.why: The HttpOnly flag stops JavaScript from reading the cookie, which limits theft of a session cookie through XSS.

quiz.q: A Content Security Policy mainly helps against…
quiz.why: A Content Security Policy restricts where scripts can load from, so it mainly helps against XSS.

quiz.q: subprocess.run(['ping', '-c', '1', host]) is safer than os.system('ping ' + host) because…
options: Arguments aren't interpreted by a shell
quiz.why: With a list of arguments and no shell, the host value is not interpreted by a shell. This prevents command injection through characters like ; or &.

story.title: The coupon that worked a thousand times

scenes.text: A grocery app in Delhi launched a ₹200 first-order coupon. Within a day, one person had used it on 1,000 orders from newly created accounts.
Security engineer Ritesh also found that a 'change email' request had no CSRF protection, and password reset tokens never expired.
They added rate limits and device signals for sign-ups, SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens, short-lived single-use reset tokens, and server-side checks for every business rule.

steps.title: Access control principles
steps.body:
- **Deny by default**; grant only what's needed (least privilege).
- Enforce on the **server** for every request — function level (is this user an admin?) and object level (does this order belong to this user?).
- Use one central, tested authorisation mechanism, not scattered checks.
- Models: role-based (RBAC), attribute-based (ABAC: rules on user, resource and context), relationship-based (who is connected to what).
- Log access-control failures and alert on patterns.

steps.title: Authentication and sessions
steps.body:
- Store passwords with Argon2/bcrypt/scrypt; support MFA and passkeys; check new passwords against known-breached lists.
- **Rate-limit** and add lockouts/backoff to slow brute force and credential stuffing.
- **Sessions:** random, long session IDs; regenerate after login; set cookies **Secure**, **HttpOnly**, **SameSite**; expire after inactivity; invalidate on logout and password change.
- **Password reset:** single-use, short-lived, random tokens sent to a verified channel; don't reveal whether an account exists.
- **JWTs:** verify signatures and algorithms, keep lifetimes short, never put secrets in the payload (it's only encoded, not encrypted, unless you use encryption).

steps.title: CSRF in brief
steps.body:
**Cross-site request forgery:** a malicious site causes the victim's browser to send an authenticated request to your site (because cookies are sent automatically).
Defences: **SameSite** cookies (Lax or Strict), anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing requests, checking the Origin/Referer header, and requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions (changing email or password).

steps.title: Worked example: a server-side business rule
steps.body:
Rule: 'first-order coupon once per person'.
- Weak: check a 'used' flag stored in the app (client) — attackers edit it.
- Better: the server checks coupon usage against the verified phone number, payment instrument and device signals; the database enforces a unique constraint on (coupon_id, verified_phone).
Abuse is a security problem too — design for how people will *misuse* features.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trusting user IDs, roles or prices sent from the client.
- Leaving old API versions running without new checks.
- Long-lived tokens with no revocation.
- Error messages like 'password wrong for this email' that help attackers enumerate accounts.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: List the three most sensitive actions in an app you know (e.g. change payout bank account). For each, write: who may do it, what checks happen server-side, and whether re-authentication is required.

activity.prompt: Authentication and session hardening checklist.

MFA or passkeys available (required for admins)
Login and OTP endpoints rate-limited
Session ID regenerated after login
Cookies set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite
Sessions expire after inactivity and on logout
Password-reset tokens are single-use and short-lived
Every object access checked on the server
Sensitive actions require re-authentication
Authorisation failures are logged and monitored

options: On the server for every request
quiz.why: Authorisation must be enforced on the server for every request. The client can always be bypassed.

quiz.q: Which cookie attribute helps most against CSRF?
quiz.why: The SameSite cookie attribute limits sending cookies on cross-site requests, which helps most against CSRF.

quiz.q: Why regenerate the session ID after login?
quiz.why: Regenerating the session ID after login prevents session fixation: an ID planted by an attacker becomes useless.

options: Encoded and signed, but readable unless separately encrypted
quiz.why: A JWT payload is encoded and signed, but anyone can read it unless it is separately encrypted. Don't put secrets in it.

quiz.q: Best error message for a failed login?
quiz.why: 'Invalid email or password' doesn't reveal which part was wrong. Specific messages help attackers find valid accounts, and stack traces leak internal details.

lessons.title: Secure development lifecycle: design, dependencies, config, logging and SSRF

scenes.text: A critical vulnerability was announced in a popular logging library. A fintech team in Pune had to find out — that night — whether they used it anywhere.
Because they kept a software bill of materials (SBOM) and ran dependency scanning in CI, engineer Sam listed every affected service in ten minutes.
They patched by morning. A competitor without an inventory spent a week searching. 'Security is mostly good engineering hygiene,' Sam's manager said.

steps.title: Shift left: security from the start
steps.body:
- **Threat modelling** during design: what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, did we do a good job? STRIDE is a common prompt list: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
- **Secure coding standards** and peer review with a security checklist.
- **Automated checks in CI:** SAST (static code analysis), dependency/SCA scanning, secret scanning, container image scanning, IaC scanning; DAST (dynamic testing of the running app) in staging.
- **Penetration tests** and bug bounties for deeper, human testing.

steps.title: Components and integrity (A06, A08)
steps.body:
- Keep an inventory (SBOM) of dependencies and versions.
- Update regularly; subscribe to advisories; remove unused packages.
- Pin versions and use lock files; verify package integrity and signatures; beware typosquatted package names.
- Protect the CI/CD pipeline: least-privilege tokens, protected branches, signed artifacts, review of pipeline changes.

steps.title: Misconfiguration and SSRF (A05, A10)
steps.body:
Misconfiguration examples: default credentials, debug mode in production, directory listing, verbose stack traces, public cloud buckets, missing security headers. Fix with hardened templates, infrastructure as code with policy checks, and regular configuration scans.
**SSRF:** if your server fetches URLs supplied by users (image previews, webhooks), attackers may target internal addresses or cloud instance metadata endpoints. Defences: allow-lists of destinations, block private and link-local IP ranges after DNS resolution, disable redirects or re-validate them, use cloud metadata protections (e.g. AWS IMDSv2), and run fetchers in isolated network segments.

steps.title: Logging and monitoring (A09)
steps.body:
- Log security-relevant events: logins (success and failure), MFA changes, permission changes, access denials, admin actions, high-value transactions.
- Include who, what, when, where (IP/device), outcome — never passwords, OTPs, full card numbers or unnecessary personal data.
- Centralise logs, protect them from tampering, set retention, and create alerts with clear owners and runbooks.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Run your language's dependency audit command on a project (npm audit, pip-audit, or your platform's scanner). Triage the results: which are reachable in your code, which need updates now, and which can wait?

quiz.why: STRIDE is a threat modelling aid. Its letters stand for types of threat: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

options: An inventory of software components and versions
quiz.why: An SBOM (software bill of materials) is an inventory of the components and versions in your software. It helps you find vulnerable ones.

quiz.q: A user-supplied URL makes your server call an internal admin endpoint. This is…
quiz.why: When a user-supplied URL makes your server call an internal endpoint, it is server-side request forgery (SSRF).

quiz.q: Which should NOT appear in security logs?
quiz.why: Plain-text passwords and OTPs must never appear in logs. Outcome, timestamp and user ID are useful and safe.
SAST (static application security testing) analyses source code without running it.

options: A non-profit community producing open security guidance
questions.why: OWASP is a non-profit community that produces open guidance on application security, such as the Top 10.

questions.q: SQL injection is prevented primarily by…
questions.why: Parameterised queries separate code from data, which prevents SQL injection.

questions.q: Accessing another user's invoice by changing an ID is…
questions.why: Changing an ID to see someone else's invoice is an IDOR, a form of broken access control (A01).

questions.q: Which header restricts where scripts can load from?
questions.why: The Content-Security-Policy header restricts where scripts and other resources can load from.

questions.q: Debug mode left on in production is…
questions.why: Debug mode left on in production is a security misconfiguration (A05). It can leak internal details.

questions.q: Using a library with a known critical vulnerability falls under…
questions.why: Using a library with a known critical vulnerability falls under A06, Vulnerable and Outdated Components.

options: Browsers automatically send cookies with cross-site requests
questions.why: CSRF works because browsers automatically send cookies with cross-site requests. SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens counter it.

questions.q: Which practice best prevents session fixation?
options: Regenerating the session ID after login
questions.why: Regenerating the session ID after login prevents session fixation. An ID set before login is replaced by a new one.

questions.q: Dynamic sort column from user input should be handled by…
options: An allow-list of permitted column names
questions.why: Column names can't be bound as query parameters. Accept only values from an allow-list of permitted names, not concatenated user text.

questions.q: Best SSRF defence for an image-preview feature?
options: Hide the feature in the UI
Allow-list destinations and block private/link-local IPs after resolution
questions.why: To prevent SSRF, allow-list the destinations and block private or link-local IPs after DNS resolution. This controls where the server can connect.

questions.q: Which belongs in a security log for a failed admin login?
questions.why: A failed admin login log should contain user, time, source IP and outcome. That's useful context without storing secrets like passwords or OTPs.

questions.q: A popular package is compromised and pushes malicious updates. Which controls help most?
options: Pinned versions, lock files, integrity checks and dependency monitoring
questions.why: A compromised package is a supply-chain attack. Pinned versions, lock files, integrity checks and dependency monitoring help catch or avoid it.

questions.q: Frontend input validation alone is insufficient because…
options: Attackers can send requests directly to the API, bypassing the UI
questions.why: Attackers can send requests directly to the API and bypass the UI, so frontend validation alone is not enough. Server-side validation and authorisation are mandatory.

courses.title: Security operations, architecture and governance (CompTIA Security+ style)
courses.summary: For aspiring security analysts: control types, secure architecture and zero trust, vulnerability management, incident response, SIEM and logs, and risk, governance and compliance — including India's incident-reporting expectations. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can classify security controls by category and type
Learners can explain zero trust, segmentation, and common network security devices
Learners can run a vulnerability management cycle and use CVSS sensibly
Learners can follow incident response phases and preserve evidence
Learners can explain risk analysis, BIA terms (RTO, RPO) and governance documents

scenes.text: A pharmaceutical manufacturer in Baddi had one flat network: office laptops, lab instruments and factory controllers could all talk to each other.
A phishing email infected one office laptop; the malware spread straight to lab systems and stopped production for two days.

Security architect Gurpreet segmented the network into zones with firewalls between them, added MFA for remote access, and moved towards zero trust: every request verified, nothing trusted just because it's 'inside'.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline, which is revised periodically.

steps.title: Control categories and types
steps.body:
**Categories (who/what implements it):**
- **Technical:** firewalls, encryption, MFA, EDR.
- **Managerial:** policies, risk assessments, security planning.
- **Operational:** procedures carried out by people — awareness training, guard patrols, change management.
- **Physical:** locks, fences, CCTV, badges.
**Types (what it does):**
- **Preventive** (stop it: MFA, firewall rule), **Deterrent** (discourage: warning banner, visible CCTV), **Detective** (find it: IDS, log review), **Corrective** (fix it: restore from backup, patch), **Compensating** (alternative when the ideal control isn't possible), **Directive** (tell people what to do: policy, signage).

steps.title: Architecture building blocks
steps.body:
- **Segmentation:** separate networks/VLANs/subnets by trust level; firewalls between zones; a **DMZ/screened subnet** for internet-facing services.
- **Firewalls** (stateful, next-generation with application awareness), **web application firewalls**, **IDS/IPS** (detect vs block), **proxies**, **VPNs**, **NAC** (network access control).
- **Zero trust:** no implicit trust based on network location; verify identity and device posture for every request; least privilege; continuous monitoring. Concepts: policy decision point and policy enforcement point.
- **Defence in depth:** multiple layers so one failure doesn't mean total compromise.
- **Secure baselines** and hardening; **high availability** and redundancy; backups (including offline/immutable).

steps.title: Worked example: classifying controls
steps.body:
- Door badge reader → physical, preventive.
- Monthly access review by managers → operational/managerial, detective.
- Restoring a server from backup after ransomware → technical, corrective.
- 'Authorised users only' login banner → deterrent (and directive).
- An old machine that can't be patched is isolated in its own VLAN → compensating control.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Walk around your office, college or home and list 10 controls you can see. Classify each by category and type.

items.text: 'This area is under CCTV surveillance' sign
Isolating an unpatchable legacy server in its own network segment

quiz.q: A security policy document is mainly a ___ control.
quiz.why: A security policy document directs behaviour, so it is a managerial (directive) control, not a technical one.

quiz.q: IDS vs IPS: an IPS can…
quiz.why: An IPS (intrusion prevention system) sits inline and can block traffic. An IDS only detects and logs.

options: Verify every request regardless of network location
quiz.why: Zero trust means verifying every request, whatever the network location. It doesn't trust anything just because it is inside the network.

quiz.q: Public web servers are often placed in a…
quiz.why: Public web servers are placed in a DMZ (screened subnet), a buffer zone between the internet and the internal network.

quiz.q: When a primary control isn't feasible, an alternative that reduces risk is a…
quiz.why: A compensating control is an alternative that reduces risk when the primary control isn't feasible.

story.title: Friday 6 p.m., the SIEM lights up

scenes.text: At a hospital group in Chennai, the SIEM alerted: a service account was logging in to dozens of servers it never normally touched.
Analyst Priya followed the incident response plan: confirm the alert, scope it, isolate the affected servers, disable the account, preserve logs and disk images.

The root cause was an unpatched VPN appliance. After recovery, the lessons-learned meeting led to faster patching SLAs for internet-facing devices — and the incident was reported to the authorities within the required time.

steps.title: Vulnerability management cycle
steps.body:
- **Inventory** assets (you can't protect what you don't know).
- **Scan and identify** (authenticated scans find more), plus threat intelligence and advisories.
- **Analyse and prioritise:** **CVSS** scores severity from 0.0 to 10.0, but also weigh exploitability (is it actively exploited?), exposure (internet-facing?), and asset criticality.
- **Remediate** (patch, configure, upgrade) or **mitigate** (compensating control) or formally **accept** with an exception and expiry.
- **Verify** by rescanning, and **report** metrics (time to remediate by severity).

steps.title: Incident response phases
steps.body:
A common model (aligned with NIST guidance):
- **Preparation:** plan, roles, contacts, tools, playbooks, training and exercises.
- **Detection and analysis:** triage alerts, confirm incidents, determine scope and severity.
- **Containment:** stop the spread (isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs) — short-term then long-term.
- **Eradication:** remove the cause (malware, backdoors, exploited vulnerability).
- **Recovery:** restore systems, monitor closely for re-infection.
- **Lessons learned / post-incident activity:** what happened, what worked, what to improve.

steps.title: Evidence and logs
steps.body:
- **Order of volatility:** collect the most volatile data first (CPU/cache and memory, then network state and running processes, then disk, then logs and backups).
- **Chain of custody:** document who handled evidence, when and how; use hashes to prove integrity.
- **Legal hold:** preserve relevant data when litigation or investigation is expected.
- **SIEM:** collects and correlates logs from many sources; **SOAR** automates response playbooks; **EDR/XDR** watches endpoints and beyond.

steps.title: Reporting in India
steps.body: India's CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) issued directions in April 2022 requiring specified cyber incidents to be reported to CERT-In within **6 hours** of noticing them, among other obligations (such as maintaining logs). Sector regulators and data-protection law may impose additional duties. Organisations should check the current requirements with their legal and compliance teams. This is general education, not legal advice.

quiz.q: Isolating an infected laptop from the network is part of…
quiz.why: Isolating an infected laptop from the network is containment: it stops the spread of the incident.

quiz.q: Which should be collected first by order of volatility?
quiz.why: By the order of volatility, collect the most volatile evidence first. System memory (RAM) is lost when power goes off.
Chain of custody records who handled evidence and how. It supports its integrity in investigations.

story.title: How long can we be down?

scenes.text: The board of a cooperative bank in Nagpur asked the new CISO, Anita: 'How much should we spend on security this year?'
She ran a business impact analysis: core banking could tolerate at most 2 hours down and 15 minutes of data loss; the HR portal could wait a day.
With those numbers, risk registers and a policy framework, the board approved a budget tied to real business risks rather than fear.

steps.title: Risk analysis
steps.body:
- **Qualitative:** rate likelihood and impact (low/medium/high) on a heat map.
- **Quantitative:** **SLE** (single loss expectancy) = asset value × exposure factor; **ARO** (annualised rate of occurrence); **ALE** (annualised loss expectancy) = SLE × ARO.
- **Risk register:** each risk with owner, rating, treatment and status. **Risk appetite/tolerance:** how much risk leadership is willing to accept.
- Treatments: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept.

steps.title: Worked example: ALE
steps.body:
A laptop worth ₹80,000 with data; if stolen, the loss (device + response costs) is estimated at ₹2,00,000 (SLE). Thefts happen about 0.5 times per year (ARO).
ALE = ₹2,00,000 × 0.5 = ₹1,00,000 per year.
A control costing ₹30,000 per year that cuts thefts' impact substantially (full-disk encryption + remote wipe + cable locks) is easy to justify.

steps.title: Business impact analysis terms
steps.body:
- **RTO (recovery time objective):** maximum acceptable time to restore a service.
- **RPO (recovery point objective):** maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (15 minutes → back up/replicate at least that often).
- **MTBF** (mean time between failures) and **MTTR** (mean time to repair) describe reliability.
- Continuity planning: business continuity plan (BCP), disaster recovery plan (DRP), and testing via tabletop exercises and failover tests. Site types: hot, warm, cold sites.

steps.title: Governance documents and frameworks
steps.body:
- **Policies** (high-level, mandatory), **standards** (specific requirements), **procedures** (step-by-step), **guidelines** (recommended).
- Frameworks and standards often referenced: ISO/IEC 27001 (information security management systems), NIST Cybersecurity Framework, CIS Controls, PCI DSS (card data).
- Privacy: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; GDPR in the EU.
- Third-party risk: vendor assessments, contracts with security clauses, right to audit, SLAs.
- Security awareness training and phishing simulations as ongoing programmes. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For one system you rely on (college ERP, a shop's billing app), propose an RTO and RPO and explain what backup or replication frequency would meet the RPO.

activity.prompt: SLE is ₹5,00,000 and ARO is 0.2 per year. What is the ALE in rupees?

quiz.why: ALE (annualised loss expectancy) = SLE (single loss expectancy) × ARO (annual rate of occurrence).

quiz.q: Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time is the…
quiz.why: RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. RTO is how quickly service must be restored.

quiz.q: Step-by-step instructions for a task are a…
quiz.why: A procedure gives detailed step-by-step instructions for a task. Policies and standards are higher level.
ISO/IEC 27001 is the standard for information security management systems (ISMS).

quiz.q: Which site type is ready to take over almost immediately?
quiz.why: A hot site is fully equipped and has current data, so it can take over almost immediately. Warm sites take longer and cold sites longest.

questions.q: A firewall is mainly a ___ control.
questions.why: A firewall blocks unwanted traffic, so it is a technical, preventive control.

questions.q: The first incident response phase is…
questions.why: The first phase of incident response is Preparation, because plans and tools must be ready before an incident.

questions.q: Maximum tolerable downtime target for a service is the…
questions.why: RTO (recovery time objective) is the target time within which a service must be restored. RPO is about data loss.

questions.q: Which tool correlates logs across many systems?
questions.why: A SIEM collects and correlates logs from many systems, so you can spot patterns and alerts.
Network segmentation limits lateral movement after a compromise, so an attacker can't easily reach the other parts.

questions.q: An unpatchable machine is isolated and monitored instead. This is a…
questions.why: Isolating and monitoring a machine that can't be patched is an alternative way to reduce risk. That is a compensating control.

questions.q: Which is collected first during forensic acquisition?
questions.why: By the order of volatility, RAM contents are collected first, since they vanish when the power goes off. Backups and printed logs last longest.

options: CVSS plus active exploitation, exposure and asset criticality
questions.why: Prioritise vulnerabilities by CVSS together with active exploitation, exposure and how critical the asset is. A score alone can mislead.
An RPO of 15 minutes means at most 15 minutes of data may be lost, so backups or replication must happen at least every 15 minutes.

questions.q: Under CERT-In's 2022 directions, specified incidents must be reported within…
questions.why: CERT-In's 2022 directions require specified incidents to be reported within 6 hours of noticing them. Rules can change, so check the current ones.

questions.q: Zero trust architectures separate the policy decision point from the…
questions.why: Zero trust separates the policy decision point, which decides, from the policy enforcement point, which enforces the decision.

questions.q: After recovering from an incident, the most valuable final step is…
options: A lessons-learned review that updates controls and playbooks
questions.why: After an incident, a lessons-learned review updates controls and playbooks. This leads to continuous improvement. Deleting logs or blaming people doesn't.
