story.title: Release day at a payments company

scenes.text: A payments company in Gurugram released software once a quarter. Release weekends meant 300 changes at once, pizza at 2 a.m., and frequent rollbacks.
New engineering head Nandini introduced small daily changes, automated tests, shared on-call between developers and operations, and blameless post-incident reviews.
A year later they deployed many times a day, with fewer failures and faster recovery. Nobody missed the 2 a.m. pizza.

steps.title: What DevOps means
steps.body:
**DevOps** is a set of cultural practices and tools that bring development and operations together to deliver software **faster and more reliably**. Core ideas:
- Shared ownership: 'you build it, you run it'.
- Small batches and frequent integration.
- Automation of builds, tests, deployments and infrastructure.
- Fast feedback from monitoring and users.
- Blameless learning from failures.
Related: **SRE** (site reliability engineering) applies software engineering to operations, using **SLOs** (service level objectives) and **error budgets**.

steps.title: The four DORA metrics
steps.body:
Research by the DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) programme identified four key delivery metrics:
- **Deployment frequency:** how often you release to production.
- **Lead time for changes:** time from commit to running in production.
- **Change failure rate:** percentage of deployments causing a failure in production.
- **Time to restore service** (also described as failed deployment recovery time): how quickly you recover from a failure.
The first two measure speed; the last two measure stability. High performers do well on both — speed and stability are not opposites.

steps.title: Worked example: computing metrics
steps.body:
In March, a team deployed 40 times; 4 deployments caused incidents; recovery took 30, 45, 15 and 90 minutes.
- Deployment frequency: 40/month (about 2 per working day).
- Change failure rate: 4/40 = 10%.
- Mean time to restore: (30+45+15+90)/4 = 45 minutes.
Track trends over months; use them to improve the system, not to blame individuals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'DevOps' as a job title or a tool purchase without changing how teams work.
- Gaming metrics (splitting deployments to inflate frequency).
- Automating a broken process instead of simplifying it first.
- Blame culture — people hide mistakes, and the same incidents repeat.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For a project you know, estimate the four DORA metrics. Which one would you improve first, and what single change would help most?

activity.prompt: A team made 25 deployments last month and 3 caused production incidents. What is the change failure rate (%)?

quiz.why: Change failure rate measures how often changes cause failures, so it measures stability. Deployment frequency and lead time measure speed.
Lead time for changes is the time from a code commit to running in production.

quiz.q: A blameless post-incident review focuses on…
quiz.why: A blameless post-incident review focuses on improving systems and processes, not on punishing a person.

options: The allowed unreliability implied by an SLO
quiz.why: An error budget is the amount of unreliability an SLO allows. For example, a 99.9% SLO gives a 0.1% budget.

options: Both high speed and high stability
quiz.why: DORA research shows that high-performing teams achieve both high speed and high stability. They are not a trade-off.

story.title: The pipeline that caught a bug at 4 p.m.

scenes.text: Developer Sameer pushed a change to the food-delivery app's pricing service. Within minutes, the pipeline's unit tests failed: a discount rounding bug.
He fixed it, the pipeline passed, deployed to staging, ran integration tests, then released to 5% of users as a canary.
Error rates stayed flat; the canary expanded to 100% automatically. No release weekend, no drama.

steps.title: CI, continuous delivery, continuous deployment
steps.body:
- **Continuous integration (CI):** everyone merges small changes frequently into a shared branch; each change automatically builds and runs tests.
- **Continuous delivery:** every change that passes the pipeline is *ready* to release; production release may need a manual approval.
- **Continuous deployment:** every passing change goes to production automatically.
A typical pipeline: checkout → build → unit tests → static analysis & security scans → package (container image) → deploy to staging → integration/end-to-end tests → approval (optional) → deploy to production → smoke tests → monitor.

steps.title: Worked example: a GitHub Actions workflow
steps.body:
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -q

Other tools follow the same idea: Azure Pipelines, GitLab CI, Jenkins — pipelines as code, stored in the repository and reviewed like code.

steps.title: Deployment strategies
steps.body:
- **Rolling:** replace instances gradually; simple; old and new versions run together briefly.
- **Blue-green:** run the new version (green) alongside the old (blue); switch traffic at once; instant rollback by switching back. Needs double capacity during release.
- **Canary:** send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, expand gradually.
- **Feature flags:** deploy code switched off; enable for selected users; separates *deploy* from *release*.
Always plan **rollback** and backward-compatible database changes (expand → migrate → contract).

steps.title: Pipeline security and hygiene
steps.body:
- Store secrets in the CI platform's secret store or a vault, never in the repository.
- Use least-privilege, short-lived credentials (e.g. OIDC federation from CI to the cloud).
- Protect the main branch: required reviews and passing checks.
- Pin third-party actions/plugins to trusted versions.
- Keep pipelines fast (aim for minutes) — slow pipelines push people to skip them.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Add a CI workflow to one of your repositories that runs tests on every pull request. Make the main branch require it to pass before merging.

activity.prompt: Match each deployment strategy to its description.
pairs: Replace instances a few at a time
Two full environments; switch traffic at once
Small share of users first, then expand
Code deployed but switched on selectively
Every passing change goes to production automatically
Every passing change is ready; release may need approval

options: Merging small changes often with automated builds and tests
Working on long-lived branches for months
quiz.why: Continuous integration means merging small changes often, with automated builds and tests. This finds problems early.

quiz.q: Which strategy allows instant rollback by switching traffic back?
quiz.why: Blue-green deployment keeps the old environment ready, so you can roll back instantly by switching traffic back.
Feature flags separate deploy from release. You can ship code switched off and turn it on later.

quiz.q: Where should a pipeline's cloud credentials live?
options: In the CI secret store or via short-lived federated credentials
quiz.why: Pipeline credentials belong in the CI secret store, or should be short-lived federated credentials. Never put them in the repo, README or Dockerfile.

quiz.q: Database changes during zero-downtime deploys should be…
quiz.why: For zero downtime, database changes must be backward-compatible (expand, migrate, contract). Old and new versions may run at the same time.

scenes.text: Intern Kriti's Python API worked on her laptop but crashed on the server: different Python version, missing system library.
Her mentor Joel showed her Docker: package the app with its runtime and libraries into an image; run the same image everywhere.
The image ran identically on her laptop, in CI and in production. 'Now it works on every machine,' Joel joked.

steps.title: Images and containers
steps.body:
- An **image** is a read-only template: a minimal file system with your app, runtime and libraries, built in **layers**.
- A **container** is a running instance of an image — an isolated process sharing the host's OS kernel (lighter than a VM, which includes a full guest OS).
- **Registries** store images (Docker Hub, Azure Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry).
- Containers should be **immutable** and **stateless**: store data in volumes or external services.

steps.title: Worked example: a Dockerfile
steps.body:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd -m appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Build and run:
docker build -t kriti-api:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:8000 --name api kriti-api:1.0
Then open http://localhost:8080. Copying requirements.txt before the rest of the code lets Docker **cache** the dependency layer when only code changes.

steps.title: Everyday commands and concepts
steps.body:
- docker ps (running containers), docker logs api, docker exec -it api sh, docker stop api, docker images.
- **Volumes** for persistent data; **networks** for container-to-container communication.
- **Docker Compose** (compose.yaml) runs multi-container apps locally: API + database + cache with one command (docker compose up).
- **Multi-stage builds:** compile in a 'builder' stage, copy only the output into a small final image.

steps.title: Container security basics
steps.body:
- Use small, trusted base images and update them regularly; scan images for vulnerabilities.
- Don't run as root (USER in the Dockerfile).
- Never bake secrets into images — they remain in image layers; inject at runtime.
- Pin image versions (python:3.12-slim, or a digest) rather than 'latest'.
- Use a .dockerignore to keep .git, .env and local files out of the build context.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Containerise a small app you've written. Check the image size, then try a slimmer base image or a multi-stage build and compare.

activity.prompt: Order the lines of a well-structured Dockerfile.
items: FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
USER appuser (after creating it)
EXPOSE 8000
CMD to start the server

quiz.q: Containers differ from VMs mainly because containers…
quiz.why: Containers share the host operating system's kernel, so they are lightweight. A VM includes a full guest OS.
In -p host:container, 8080:8000 maps host port 8080 to container port 8000.

quiz.q: Why copy requirements.txt before the rest of the code?
options: To reuse the cached dependency layer when only code changes
quiz.why: Copying requirements.txt first lets Docker reuse the cached dependency layer when only the code changes. This makes rebuilds faster.

options: Injected at runtime from a secret store
quiz.why: Database passwords should be injected at runtime from a secret store. Image layers persist secrets, so baking them in leaks them.

quiz.q: Run a local app with an API, a database and a cache together — use…
quiz.why: Docker Compose runs several containers, like an API, database and cache, together locally from one file.

scenes.text: An e-commerce platform in Bengaluru grew to 40 containerised services. Restarting crashed containers and scaling them by hand kept engineer Faisal up at night.
They moved to managed Kubernetes. Deployments kept the desired number of replicas running, Services gave stable addresses, and autoscaling handled sales.
When a node failed at 3 a.m., Kubernetes rescheduled the pods elsewhere. Faisal slept through it.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.body:
A **cluster** has a **control plane** and **worker nodes**.
- Control plane: **API server** (front door for kubectl and everything else), **etcd** (key-value store of cluster state), **scheduler** (places pods on nodes), **controller manager** (reconciles desired vs actual state).
- Nodes: **kubelet** (runs pods), **kube-proxy** (service networking), container runtime.
Managed services (AKS, EKS, GKE) run the control plane for you.
Kubernetes is **declarative**: you describe the desired state in YAML; controllers continuously make reality match it.

steps.title: Core objects
steps.body:
- **Pod:** smallest unit; one or more containers sharing network and storage.
- **Deployment:** manages ReplicaSets to keep N identical pods running; rolling updates and rollbacks.
- **Service:** stable virtual IP/DNS name for a set of pods — **ClusterIP** (internal), **NodePort**, **LoadBalancer** (cloud load balancer).
- **Ingress** (or the newer Gateway API): HTTP routing from outside to services.
- **ConfigMap** (configuration) and **Secret** (sensitive values — base64-encoded, so enable encryption at rest and restrict access, or use an external secret store).
- **Namespace:** logical separation; **StatefulSet** for stateful apps; **DaemonSet** for one pod per node; **Job/CronJob** for batch.

steps.title: Worked example: a Deployment and Service
Health, scaling and resources
steps.body:
- **Readiness probe:** only send traffic when ready. **Liveness probe:** restart if stuck. (Startup probes for slow starters.)
- **Requests** (guaranteed resources used for scheduling) and **limits** (caps).
- **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA):** scale replicas on CPU, memory or custom metrics; **cluster autoscaler** adds nodes.
- Debugging: kubectl describe pod, kubectl logs, kubectl get events. Common states: CrashLoopBackOff (app keeps crashing), ImagePullBackOff (can't pull the image), Pending (no node has enough resources).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No readiness probe → users hit pods that aren't ready.
- No resource requests → poor scheduling and noisy neighbours.
- Treating Secrets as encrypted by default.
- Running everything in the default namespace with broad permissions; use RBAC and network policies.
- Kubernetes for a tiny app that would be simpler on a PaaS or serverless container service.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Run a local cluster (kind or minikube), apply the Deployment above with a public sample image, scale it to 5 replicas, delete a pod and watch Kubernetes replace it.

activity.prompt: Match the Kubernetes object to its job.
pairs: Smallest deployable unit of one or more containers
Keeps N replicas running with rolling updates
Stable network name/IP for a set of pods
HTTP routing from outside into services
Changes replica count based on metrics

quiz.q: Which component stores the cluster's state?
quiz.why: etcd is the key-value store that holds the cluster's state in Kubernetes.

options: The image can't be pulled (wrong name/tag or no registry permission)
quiz.why: ImagePullBackOff means the image can't be pulled, often from a wrong image name or tag, or missing registry permission.

options: Base64-encoded; enable encryption at rest and restrict access
quiz.why: Kubernetes Secrets are only Base64-encoded by default, and encoding is not encryption. Enable encryption at rest and restrict access.

quiz.q: Which probe decides whether a pod receives traffic?
quiz.why: The readiness probe decides whether a pod receives traffic. A liveness probe decides whether to restart it.

quiz.q: Roll back a bad Deployment quickly with…
quiz.why: kubectl rollout undo deployment/web rolls the deployment back to its previous revision, using the built-in rollout history.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code, GitOps and DevSecOps

story.title: The click-ops environment nobody could rebuild

scenes.text: A logistics company's production environment had been built by clicking in the cloud portal over three years. When a region had problems, nobody could rebuild it elsewhere.
Platform lead Aarti's team described everything in Terraform, stored in Git, reviewed through pull requests, and applied by a pipeline.
Six months later they recreated the full environment in a second region in an afternoon — and spotted manual 'drift' changes automatically.

steps.title: Infrastructure as code (IaC)
steps.body:
IaC describes infrastructure in files that are versioned, reviewed and applied automatically.
- **Declarative** tools (Terraform/OpenTofu, Bicep/ARM, CloudFormation, Pulumi in declarative style) describe the desired end state.
- Benefits: repeatability, review, audit trail, disaster recovery, consistent environments.
- **Configuration management** tools (Ansible, Chef, Puppet) configure software inside servers.

steps.title: Worked example: Terraform workflow
GitOps
steps.body: **GitOps** uses Git as the single source of truth for desired state. An agent in the cluster (e.g. Argo CD or Flux) continuously compares Git with the live system and reconciles differences. Changes happen through pull requests, giving review, history and easy rollback (revert the commit). **Drift** — manual changes made outside the process — is detected and corrected.

steps.title: DevSecOps: security in every step
steps.body:
- **Plan:** threat modelling.
- **Code:** secure coding, pre-commit secret scanning.
- **Build:** SAST, dependency scanning (SCA), SBOM generation, image scanning, signing artifacts.
- **Infrastructure:** IaC scanning and policy as code (e.g. Open Policy Agent, cloud policy services) to block insecure settings like public storage.
- **Deploy:** least-privilege pipeline identities, approvals for production.
- **Run:** runtime monitoring, vulnerability management, incident response.
Goal: fast feedback so security issues are fixed when they're cheapest — early.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Local state files on a laptop — lost or conflicting state.
- Applying without reading the plan (that 'destroy 12 resources' line matters!).
- Hard-coding secrets in .tf files or variables committed to Git.
- Mixing manual portal changes with IaC, causing drift.
- One giant state for everything — split by environment/component to limit blast radius.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write Terraform (or Bicep) for a resource group and a storage account in a practice subscription. Run plan, apply, change a tag, plan again, then destroy. Notice how the plan explains every change.

a.text: You are Aarti. A teammate fixed production by changing a firewall rule in the portal at 2 a.m. What next?

choices.label: Capture the change in Terraform via a pull request so code matches reality
choices.feedback: Right — otherwise the next apply may revert the fix or drift persists.

choices.label: Leave it; it works
choices.feedback: Drift means the next terraform apply may undo the fix.

b.text: The plan for your PR says: '~ update 1, - destroy 1'. You expected only an update. What do you do?

choices.label: Stop and investigate the destroy before applying
choices.feedback: Always read the plan; unexpected destroys are red flags.

choices.label: Apply — it's probably fine
choices.feedback: Risky: you might delete a production resource.

c.text: Next week's routine apply reverts the firewall rule; the outage returns.

choices.label: Codify the fix in Terraform

e.text: A production database subnet association is removed; the app loses database access.

choices.label: Revert via Git, re-apply, add plan review rules
choices.feedback: Recover and add a guardrail (required approvals on destroys).

d.text: The destroy came from a renamed resource; you use a moved block/state move to preserve it. Code, state and reality agree, and the team adds required approvals for plans containing destroys.

quiz.q: Which command previews Terraform changes without making them?
quiz.why: terraform plan previews the changes Terraform would make without applying them. terraform apply actually makes the changes, and destroy removes resources.

quiz.q: Why store Terraform state remotely with locking?
options: Teams share one consistent state and avoid concurrent corrupting applies
quiz.why: Remote state with locking lets the whole team share one consistent state. The lock stops two people applying at the same time and corrupting the state.

quiz.q: In GitOps, the source of truth is…
quiz.why: In GitOps, Git is the source of truth for the desired state. An agent keeps reconciling the live system to match what is in Git.

options: Infrastructure differs from what code describes
quiz.why: Drift is when the real infrastructure differs from what the code describes, usually because of manual changes outside IaC.

quiz.q: Blocking public storage buckets automatically in pipelines is an example of…
quiz.why: Automatically blocking public buckets in the pipeline is policy as code: rules written as code and enforced automatically.

questions.q: Which DORA metric measures how often you release?
questions.why: Deployment frequency is the DORA metric for how often you release to production. Lead time measures how long a change takes.
The FROM line in a Dockerfile names the base image that your image is built on.

questions.q: Which Kubernetes object gives pods a stable network endpoint?
questions.why: A Kubernetes Service gives a set of pods a stable network endpoint (name and IP), even when the pods change.

options: Every passing change goes to production automatically
questions.why: Continuous deployment means every change that passes the automated tests goes to production automatically. Continuous delivery still has a manual release step.

questions.q: Which tool family describes infrastructure declaratively?
questions.why: Terraform, Bicep and CloudFormation are infrastructure-as-code tools, which describe infrastructure declaratively in files.

options: Releasing to all users at once
Releasing to a small share first and watching metrics
questions.why: A canary deployment releases to a small share of users first and watches metrics. If it looks bad, the damage is small.

questions.q: Why not use the 'latest' tag in production manifests?
questions.why: The 'latest' tag changes over time, so it is ambiguous and not reproducible. Pin a specific version or digest in production.

questions.q: A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. First diagnostic step?
options: kubectl logs and kubectl describe pod
questions.why: For CrashLoopBackOff, first read the container's logs and the pod's events with kubectl logs and kubectl describe pod. These show why it keeps exiting.

questions.q: 40 deployments, 2 caused incidents. Change failure rate?
questions.why: Change failure rate = failed deployments ÷ total deployments = 2/40 = 5%.

questions.q: Secrets baked into an image layer and later deleted in another layer are…
options: Still recoverable from the earlier layer
questions.why: Image layers keep history. A secret added in one layer and deleted in a later one is still recoverable from the earlier layer.

questions.q: Terraform plan shows an unexpected destroy of a database after renaming its resource block. Best fix?
options: Use a moved block / state move so Terraform maps the old resource to the new name
questions.why: Renaming a resource block makes Terraform think the old one is gone and a new one is needed, so it plans to destroy the database. A moved block or state move maps the old resource to the new name.

questions.q: Which probe should restart a hung container?
questions.why: A liveness probe checks whether the container is still healthy, and Kubernetes restarts it when it fails. A readiness probe controls traffic instead.

questions.q: Best way for a CI pipeline to deploy to the cloud without long-lived secrets?
options: OIDC federation issuing short-lived credentials to the pipeline
Store an admin password in the repo
questions.why: OIDC federation gives the pipeline short-lived credentials, so no long-lived secret is stored. Passwords in the repo or shared accounts are unsafe.

questions.q: Speed and stability in DORA research are…
questions.why: DORA research found that high performers achieve both speed and stability. They are not a trade-off.

lessons.title: SOC roles and the SIEM pipeline

scenes.text: At 02:00 a SIEM alert fires: 'Multiple failed logons followed by success'. Tier-1 analyst Isha has ten minutes to decide if it is real.
She follows the pipeline: log source -> collection -> normalisation -> correlation -> alert -> triage -> escalate or close.

steps.title: SOC
steps.body: A Security Operations Centre monitors, detects, investigates and coordinates response. Typical tiers: **Tier 1** triage, **Tier 2** investigation, **Tier 3 / hunt / detection engineering**, plus an incident manager and threat-intel function. Metrics: **MTTD** (time to detect) and **MTTR** (time to respond/resolve).

steps.title: SIEM pipeline
steps.body: Log sources (firewalls, DNS, endpoints, identity, cloud, email) are **collected** by agents/syslog/API, **parsed and normalised** to a common schema, **enriched** (asset, user, geo, threat intel), **correlated** by rules, and stored for search. Time sync (NTP) and consistent time zones (UTC) make timelines reliable.

steps.title: Alert outcomes
steps.body: **True positive** (real malicious activity), **false positive** (benign but flagged), **benign true positive** (real but expected, e.g. a pen test), **false negative** (missed). Tuning reduces false positives without creating false negatives.

steps.title: Defensive scope
steps.body: Everything here is defensive analysis: reading logs, triaging alerts and responding. Work only on systems and data you are authorised to examine. Hosts, users and addresses in these labs are invented (documentation ranges, contoso.local, example.com).

activity.prompt: Match the SOC term.
pairs: Mapping logs to a common schema
Adding context such as asset owner or threat intel

scenes.text: Three alerts are waiting. Isha sorts them by likely verdict.

steps.title: Triage questions
steps.body: What fired? What asset/user? Is it expected? Is there corroborating evidence in another log source? What is the impact if true? Decide: close (with reason), escalate, or request more info.

steps.title: Defensive scope
steps.body: Everything here is defensive analysis: reading logs, triaging alerts and responding. Work only on systems and data you are authorised to examine. Hosts, users and addresses in these labs are invented (documentation ranges, contoso.local, example.com).

steps.title: Work like a professional
steps.body: Write down what you expect before you run a command or a calculation, then compare it with the result. Mismatches are where learning happens.

items.text: Vulnerability scanner IP 10.0.9.20 probing ports (scheduled scan, change ticket CHG-5521)

Admin runs PowerShell on a patch server during the maintenance window

steps.title: Types
steps.body: **Strategic** (trends and risk for leaders), **operational** (campaigns, actor behaviour), **tactical** (specific IOCs and TTPs for detection), **technical** (raw indicators).

steps.title: Pyramid of Pain
steps.body: From trivial to painful for the attacker: **hash values**, IP addresses, domain names, network/host artifacts, tools, and **TTPs** (tactics, techniques, procedures). Detecting behaviours at the top forces attackers to change how they work; blocking a hash costs them a recompile.

steps.title: ATT&CK
steps.body: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics (the why) and techniques (the how), e.g. Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Credential Access, Exfiltration. Technique examples: T1566 Phishing, T1110 Brute Force, T1078 Valid Accounts, T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Treating a feed as truth: indicators age quickly and may be shared infrastructure; always check confidence, age and context.

steps.title: Order of volatility
steps.body: Collect the most volatile first: CPU registers/cache, **RAM**, network connections and ARP/routing tables, running processes, **disk**, remote logging/monitoring data, archival media. Powering off loses memory.

steps.title: Chain of custody
steps.body: A record of who handled evidence, when, why and where it was stored, from collection to court/closure. Evidence bags/labels, signed hand-overs, secure storage.

lessons.title: How HA decides a host failed

scenes.text: esx07 lost both power supplies at 03:12. By 03:15 its VMs were running on other hosts.
Who decided, and how?

steps.title: FDM
steps.body: Each host runs the **FDM** agent. One host is elected **primary**; the others are secondaries. The primary monitors secondaries via **network heartbeats** (management vmk) and **datastore heartbeats** (by default 2 heartbeat datastores).

steps.title: Three situations
steps.body:
- **Failed**: no network or datastore heartbeats and no ping response → restart its VMs elsewhere.
- **Isolated**: host is alive but cannot reach other hosts nor its **isolation address** (default gateway) → applies the **isolation response** (Disabled, Shut down and restart VMs, Power off and restart VMs).
- **Partitioned**: groups of hosts can't talk to each other but each group is still up; a new primary may be elected per partition.

steps.title: HA is not zero downtime
steps.body: HA **restarts** VMs (minutes of downtime; guest reboots). For zero-downtime of a single VM, Fault Tolerance exists with strict limits. Applications still need their own clustering for app-level failures.

- **Slot policy** (based on largest reservations; conservative).
- **Dedicated failover hosts** (idle standby hosts).

courses.summary: Balance clusters with DRS: automation levels, migration threshold, affinity/anti-affinity rules, shares/reservations/limits, and the resource-pool share-dilution trap.

steps.title: Automation levels
steps.body:
- **Manual**: recommendations only.
- **Partially automated**: automatic initial placement; migrations are recommendations.
- **Fully automated**: placement and migrations automatic.
Migration threshold 1 (conservative) … 5 (aggressive); default 3. Since vSphere 7, DRS optimises a per-VM **DRS score** (how well each VM gets its resources).

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- VM-VM **affinity** (keep together) and **anti-affinity** (keep apart, e.g. two domain controllers).
- VM-Host rules: **must** / **should** run (or not run) on a host group.
Use 'should' unless there is a hard licensing or compliance reason.

steps.title: Predictive & other features
steps.body: DRS also does initial placement at power-on and works with maintenance mode evacuation.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Shares**: relative priority *only under contention*. High:Normal:Low = **4:2:1**.
- **Reservation**: guaranteed minimum.
- **Limit**: hard cap (even if resources are free!).
- **Expandable reservation**: a pool may borrow reservation from its parent.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Prod High (4) vs Dev Low (1) → Prod gets 4/5 = **80 GHz**, Dev 1/5 = **20 GHz** when both demand everything.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Limits cause throttling and ballooning even on idle hosts. Avoid unless you mean it (e.g. noisy tenant).

steps.title: Counters
steps.body:
- **%USED / %RUN**: time vCPUs ran.
- **%RDY (ready)**: time a vCPU was ready to run but waited for a physical CPU → contention.
- **%CSTP (co-stop)**: time vCPUs were held to keep sibling vCPUs in step → often oversized VMs.

steps.title: vCenter ready summation

steps.title: From cheap to expensive
steps.body:
1. **Transparent Page Sharing (TPS)**: dedupes identical pages; by default **within a VM only** (inter-VM sharing disabled by default for security since 2014 'salting').
2. **Ballooning**: VMware Tools balloon driver (vmmemctl) asks the guest to give back memory; guest chooses what to page out.
3. **Memory compression**: compress pages into a per-VM cache instead of swapping.
4. **Hypervisor swapping** to .vswp: slowest; host picks pages without guest knowledge.
(Host swap cache on SSD can soften swapping.)

steps.title: Host memory states
steps.body: High → Clear → Soft → Hard → Low as free memory falls; reclamation becomes more aggressive at each step (ballooning first, compression/swapping in hard/low).

steps.title: Limits again
steps.body: A VM **memory limit** below its configured RAM causes ballooning/swap even when the host has plenty free. It is a classic hidden misconfiguration.

steps.title: Layers

scenes.text: The backup tool takes a snapshot every night — so are snapshots backups after all?

steps.title: VADP flow
steps.body: Backup software uses the **vSphere Storage APIs – Data Protection (VADP)**: 1) take a (quiesced) snapshot, 2) read the frozen base disk via transport (hot-add, NBD/NBDSSL, SAN), 3) use **Changed Block Tracking (CBT)** to copy only changed blocks for incrementals, 4) delete the snapshot.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body:
- Crash-consistent: like pulling power.
- **Application-consistent**: VMware Tools/VSS quiesces apps (SQL, Exchange) before the snapshot.
Databases may also need log truncation handled by the backup tool.

steps.title: Policy
steps.body: **RPO** = how much data you can lose (time). **RTO** = how fast you must restore. **3-2-1-1-0**: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite, 1 offline/immutable, 0 errors in restore tests.

steps.title: What is a hypervisor?
steps.body:
A **hypervisor** is a thin layer of software that creates and runs **virtual machines (VMs)**. Each VM believes it has its own CPU, memory, disk and network card.

- **Type 1 (bare-metal)** runs directly on hardware: ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM.
- **Type 2 (hosted)** runs as an app on a normal OS: VMware Workstation, VirtualBox.

ESXi is type 1: the VMkernel schedules CPU, manages memory and owns the drivers.

steps.title: How resources map
steps.body:
- **vCPU**: a scheduling slot; the VMkernel places it on a physical core/thread when the VM needs to run.
- **vRAM**: guest 'physical' memory, backed by host RAM (and, under pressure, by balloon, compression or swap).
- **Virtual disk (VMDK)**: a file on a datastore (VMFS, NFS, vSAN, vVols).
- **vNIC**: connects to a port group on a virtual switch, which uplinks to physical NICs.

Hardware assistance (Intel VT-x / AMD-V, EPT/RVI) lets guests run most instructions at near-native speed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking more vCPUs always = faster. Over-sized VMs wait longer to be scheduled.
- Forgetting that a host failure now takes down *many* workloads: you need HA and spare capacity.
- Treating snapshots as backups (they are not; covered later).

story.title: How many hosts do we buy?

steps.title: Worked method
steps.body:
1. Demand = 40 × 4 cores × 25% = **40 cores** of real work.
2. Usable per host = 32 × 70% = **22.4 cores**.
3. Hosts for load = 40 ÷ 22.4 = 1.79 → round up to **2**.
4. Add **N+1** so one host can fail or be patched: **3 hosts**.

Repeat the same maths for memory; the bigger answer wins.

steps.title: Memory check
steps.body: 40 servers using 12 GB each = 480 GB. Hosts with 512 GB, planned to 80% = 409.6 GB usable → 480 ÷ 409.6 = 1.17 → 2 hosts, +1 = 3. CPU and RAM agree on 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sizing on peaks of every server at once (over-buys) or on averages without headroom (under-buys).
- Forgetting growth (add 20–30% for 3 years) and N+1.
- Ignoring that maintenance windows also remove a host.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.body:
- **Principal**: a user or group from an identity source (vsphere.local, Active Directory over LDAPS, or identity federation e.g. ADFS/Entra ID).
- **Privilege**: a single action (e.g. *Virtual machine > Interaction > Power on*).
- **Role**: a named set of privileges (Administrator, Read-only, No access, custom roles).
- **Permission**: principal + role assigned on an object, optionally **propagated** to children.

steps.title: Rules of thumb
steps.body:
- A permission set on a child object overrides the one inherited from the parent.
- If a user is in several groups with permissions on the same object, the privileges combine.
- **No access** explicitly blocks.
- **Global permissions** apply across all vCenters in the SSO domain and to solutions like tags/content libraries.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Granting Administrator to individuals instead of AD groups; forgetting 'Propagate to children'; using the SSO administrator account for daily work.

courses.title: Standard switches (vSS) & VMkernel networking
courses.summary: Build per-host standard switches, port groups, VLAN tagging, NIC teaming and VMkernel adapters, and test jumbo frames end-to-end.
outcomes: Learners can explain vSS, port groups, uplinks and VMkernel adapters
Learners can choose VLAN tagging mode (EST/VST/VGT) and teaming policy

scenes.text: A packet leaves web01's vNIC. Fatima, the network admin, asks the vSphere team: 'which cable does it use?'
They draw: vNIC → port group → vSwitch → uplink vmnic → physical switch port.

steps.title: Pieces
steps.body:
- **vSphere Standard Switch (vSS)**: configured per host; each host must be set up identically.
- **Port group**: policy container (VLAN ID, security, teaming, shaping) that VM vNICs connect to.
- **VMkernel adapter (vmkN)**: host's own IP interface; enable services per adapter: Management, vMotion, Provisioning, Fault Tolerance logging, vSAN, vSphere Replication, NVMe over TCP/RDMA.
- **Uplinks**: physical NICs (vmnicN). A vSwitch does not forward between its uplinks, so it cannot create a loop like a bridging switch.

steps.title: VLAN tagging modes
steps.body:
- **EST** (VLAN ID 0): physical switch tags; port is access.
- **VST** (1–4094): vSwitch tags; physical port is a trunk. Most common.
- **VGT** (4095 on vSS): the guest OS tags; use for appliances that need many VLANs.

steps.title: Teaming (load balancing)
steps.body: Route based on originating virtual port (default), source MAC hash, IP hash (requires a static EtherChannel on the physical switch), explicit failover order. Plus failover detection (link status or beacon probing) and notify switches.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.body: The vDS is **defined in vCenter** (management plane); each host keeps a hidden copy (**data plane**) that forwards traffic even if vCenter is down. Port groups are **distributed port groups**; uplinks are abstracted as Uplink1..N mapped to vmnics per host.

steps.title: VMFS-6
steps.body: Clustered file system: many hosts mount the same LUN; on-disk locking (ATS on VAAI arrays) prevents two hosts writing the same VM files. Max datastore 64 TB, VMDK up to 62 TB, 1 MB file block size, **automatic space reclamation (UNMAP)**, support for 512e and 4Kn devices.

steps.title: Facts

scenes.text: The SAN contract renews next year. The CIO asks about vSAN.
Local disks in each host pooled into one datastore.

steps.title: What vSAN is
steps.body: vSAN pools local SSD/NVMe across cluster hosts into one **vsanDatastore**. Objects (VMDK, namespace, swap) are split into components placed on different hosts by a **storage policy**. Needs a VMkernel adapter tagged for vSAN on each host (10 GbE+; ESA needs 25 GbE+).

steps.title: OSA vs ESA
steps.body:
- **OSA** (Original Storage Architecture): **disk groups** = 1 cache device + 1–7 capacity devices.
- **ESA** (Express Storage Architecture, vSphere 8): single-tier **storage pool** of NVMe devices, no cache tier, more efficient RAID-5/6 and compression by default.
- Minimum 3 hosts for a standard cluster; 2-node clusters use a **witness** appliance.

steps.title: Policies (OSA)
steps.body:
FTT = failures to tolerate.
- FTT=1 RAID-1: 2 copies + witness → **3 hosts**, 2× capacity.
- FTT=1 RAID-5: **4 hosts**, 1.33×.
- FTT=2 RAID-1: **5 hosts**, 3×.
- FTT=2 RAID-6: **6 hosts**, 1.5×.

steps.title: Rebuild headroom

- **PSA**: framework for multipathing plugins.
- **NMP** (Native Multipathing Plugin) with **SATP** (array-type handling: e.g. VMW_SATP_ALUA, VMW_SATP_DEFAULT_AA) and **PSP** (path choice).
- **HPP** (High-Performance Plugin): default for local NVMe and NVMe-oF.
- Third-party MPPs from array vendors also exist.

steps.title: PSPs
steps.body:
- **VMW_PSP_MRU**: most recently used; stays on a path until it fails.
- **VMW_PSP_FIXED**: preferred path, returns to it when restored.
- **VMW_PSP_RR**: round robin across active (optimised) paths; vendors often recommend switching paths every **1 I/O** (iops=1).
